stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Economists have long assumed that raising the minimum wage pushes employers to cut jobs. However, a growing body of research suggests that the effect may be smaller than predicted. In a study of restaurants on either side of a state border, economist Lena Okafor found that employment in the state that raised its wage grew at nearly the same rate as employment in the neighboring state that did not. Okafor argues that employers often absorb higher wages through lower staff turnover rather than through layoffs.
choices: Okafor's study confirmed the long-held assumption that higher minimum wages lead employers to cut jobs.
Restaurants in the state that raised its minimum wage saw their employment grow during the study.
Research suggests that raising the minimum wage may reduce employment less than economists have expected.
Raising the minimum wage reliably increases employment because workers leave their jobs less often.
explanation: The word 'However' marks the turn in this passage. The old assumption is set up so it can be questioned, and Okafor's border study is the evidence for the newer view. Choice C covers the assumption, the challenge to it and the study, and it keeps the passage's hedge ('may').

A.why: You took the assumption in the first sentence for the conclusion. Okafor's findings challenge that assumption. They don't confirm it.

B.why: You picked a detail from the study that is roughly accurate. It describes one result, but it leaves out the passage's point that this result challenges a long-held assumption.

D.why: You stretched the claim too far. The passage says job losses may be smaller than expected. It never says higher wages reliably increase employment.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Many endurance athletes believe that stretching before a race helps prevent injury. Researchers at a Norwegian sports institute tested this belief by assigning 300 recreational runners to either a stretching routine or a light jogging warm-up for twelve weeks. The two groups reported almost identical numbers of injuries. The researchers concluded that pre-race stretching, though popular, appears to offer little protection against injury.
choices: The runners in the study followed their assigned warm-up routines for a period of twelve weeks.
A study found that stretching before running does little to prevent injury, despite a common belief.
Light jogging is the most effective warm-up for runners who want to avoid injury before a race.
Most endurance athletes have stopped stretching before races because they doubt it prevents injury.
explanation: The last sentence sums up the passage: stretching before a race, though popular, offers little protection against injury. Choice B covers both the common belief and the study's finding that undercuts it.

A.why: You chose a true detail about how the study was set up. The length of the study isn't what the passage is trying to show.

C.why: You went beyond the evidence. The two groups had about the same number of injuries, so the study doesn't show that jogging works better than stretching, let alone that it's the most effective warm-up.

D.why: You reversed what the passage says about athletes. It says many of them believe stretching prevents injury, not that they have stopped doing it.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: For decades, archaeologists credited the stone terraces at a hillside site in the Andes to the Inca, who controlled the region in the fifteenth century. However, recent radiocarbon dating of charcoal buried beneath the lowest terrace walls indicates that the terraces were built roughly three hundred years before the Inca arrived. The findings suggest that an earlier, less well-documented community was responsible for the construction.
choices: The Inca controlled the Andean region where the stone terraces are found during the fifteenth century.
Radiocarbon dating shows that the Inca borrowed their farming methods from earlier Andean communities.
Recent evidence confirms that the Inca built the terraces soon after they arrived in the region.
New dating evidence suggests that the terraces were built by a community that predated the Inca.
explanation: The passage opens with the old view that the Inca built the terraces, then turns with 'However' to the dating evidence. What comes after the turn is the author's point: an earlier community probably built them. Choice D says this and keeps the hedge ('suggests').

A.why: You picked background from the first sentence. It's accurate, but the passage mentions it only to set up the older view that the new evidence corrects.

B.why: You added a claim the passage never makes. The dating shows when the terraces were built, not whether the Inca borrowed anyone's farming methods.

C.why: You stopped at the older view. The dating places the terraces about three hundred years before the Inca arrived, so it undercuts that view.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Engineers are increasingly using recycled materials to make road surfaces more durable. For example, a team in the Netherlands mixed shredded plastic waste into the asphalt of a two-kilometer test road. After three years of heavy truck traffic, the plastic-blend section showed about half as many cracks as a conventional section laid at the same time, and it cost no more to build.
choices: Recycled materials can help make road surfaces more durable, as one Dutch test road illustrates.
Shredded plastic is now the standard ingredient in asphalt roads throughout the Netherlands.
The Dutch test road was two kilometers long and carried heavy truck traffic for three years.
Roads made with recycled plastic cracked more often than conventional roads but cost less to build.
explanation: The first sentence makes a general claim, and 'For example' brings in a single case that supports it. Choice A covers both the claim and the test road that illustrates it.

B.why: You turned one test road into a nationwide standard. The passage describes a single experiment, not a common practice.

C.why: You repeated accurate details about the test road. They describe the example but not the claim the example supports.

D.why: You got the results backward. The plastic-blend road had about half as many cracks, and it cost the same to build, not less.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Fermented foods such as yogurt and kimchi contain live bacteria, and some researchers have proposed that eating them may strengthen the immune system. In a small trial, adults who ate several servings of fermented foods daily for ten weeks showed lower levels of certain inflammation markers than adults who did not. The researchers caution, however, that the trial was brief and that larger studies are needed before such foods can be recommended for immune health.
choices: Yogurt and kimchi are among the fermented foods that researchers say contain live bacteria.
Eating fermented foods daily has been proven to protect adults from illnesses linked to inflammation.
A small trial offers early support for fermented foods aiding immunity, but more research is needed.
The trial found that fermented foods had no measurable effect on the inflammation levels of adults.
explanation: The hedge words ('may', 'small', 'brief', 'larger studies are needed') limit how strong the claim can be. The passage reports a promising result and then warns that it isn't conclusive. Choice C includes both the promise and the warning.

A.why: You picked a background fact from the first sentence. It names the foods but says nothing about the trial or the researchers' caution.

B.why: You ignored the hedges. The researchers say more studies are needed, so nothing has been 'proven', and the trial measured inflammation markers, not illnesses.

D.why: You reversed the result. Adults who ate fermented foods had lower levels of some inflammation markers, which is a measurable effect.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Immunologists have long assumed that innate immune cells such as macrophages, unlike T cells and B cells, keep no memory of past infections. Recent work suggests that this view is incomplete. In a study led by immunologist Rafaela Okonjo, mice whose macrophages had been exposed to a harmless fungal compound responded more quickly to an unrelated bacterial infection weeks later. The macrophages appeared to keep a kind of readiness from their earlier encounter, an effect researchers now call "trained immunity."
choices: Okonjo's study found that macrophages lose any readiness from an earlier encounter within a few weeks.
Research suggests that innate immune cells may keep a form of memory, which challenges a long-held assumption.
In Okonjo's study, the macrophages of mice were exposed to a harmless compound taken from a fungus.
Trained immunity makes innate immune cells just as effective as T cells and B cells at fighting infections.
explanation: The passage sets up an old assumption (innate cells have no memory), says it is incomplete, and then gives Okonjo's study as evidence that macrophages can keep a kind of readiness. Choice B covers both parts: the evidence and the assumption it challenges. Its hedge ('suggests', 'may') matches the passage's 'suggests' and 'appeared to'.

A.why: You reversed the finding. The macrophages responded more quickly weeks later, so they kept their readiness rather than losing it.

C.why: This detail is accurate, but it only describes how the study was set up. It leaves out what the study found and why that finding matters, so it is too narrow to be the main idea.

D.why: The passage never compares how effective innate cells are with T cells and B cells. You stretched 'a kind of readiness' into a much bigger claim than the text supports.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: The fiddle tunes of the Ardel Valley have usually been described as a purely local tradition, handed down from player to player within the valley for generations. However, musicologist Tomas Brenner has found that several of the region's best-known melodies closely match dance tunes printed in a 1790s songbook from a port city two hundred miles away. Brenner argues that the valley's music, though shaped by local players, likely drew in part on printed sources from beyond the region.
choices: The Ardel Valley's fiddle tradition developed entirely within the valley, without any outside influence.
A songbook printed in a distant port city during the 1790s included a number of popular dance tunes.
Most folk music traditions that seem local actually began as tunes printed in city songbooks.
Evidence suggests that the Ardel Valley's fiddle tunes likely drew in part on music from outside the region.
explanation: The word 'However' signals the real point. The passage first gives the usual view that the tradition is purely local, then presents Brenner's evidence and conclusion that the tunes likely drew in part on outside printed sources. Choice D states that conclusion with the same level of caution as the passage ('likely', 'in part').

A.why: This is the view the passage sets up only to correct. Everything after 'However' argues against it, so you chose the opposite of the author's point.

B.why: The songbook is one piece of evidence, not the point it supports. This choice never mentions the Ardel Valley tunes or Brenner's conclusion, so it is too narrow.

C.why: The passage discusses only one region's tunes. You stretched one case into a claim about most folk traditions, and the text never makes that claim.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: In the 1850s, surveyor Ines Calloway set out to map the Merrow River delta, a maze of channels that changed shape from year to year. She measured channel depths by hand, recorded which channels shifted after floods, and asked local boat pilots about routes that opened and closed with the seasons. Because she documented how the delta moved rather than fixing it at a single moment, her map stayed useful to navigators for decades after other maps of the delta had gone out of date.
choices: Calloway's map stayed useful for decades because it recorded how the delta changed over time.
Calloway asked local boat pilots about routes that opened and closed with the seasons.
Calloway's methods became the standard for mapmakers of river deltas around the world.
Calloway's map soon went out of date because the delta's channels shifted after floods.
explanation: The middle sentence lists Calloway's methods, and the last sentence sums them up: because she recorded how the delta moved, her map stayed useful for decades. Choice A states that verdict and the reason for it, so it covers the whole passage.

B.why: This is true, but it is only one of the three methods in the middle sentence. It leaves out the result the passage builds toward, so it is too narrow.

C.why: The passage says only that her map stayed useful to navigators of this one delta. It never says that other mapmakers anywhere adopted her methods.

D.why: You reversed the outcome. Other maps went out of date, but Calloway's stayed useful because she accounted for the shifting channels.
